course.title: Causal & Statistical Reasoning
course.description: How to reason honestly with data: telling correlation from causation, spotting confounders, judging experiments and samples, and seeing through the fallacies that fool careful people. Structure adapted from Carnegie Mellon University's Open Learning Initiative (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0); all explanations original.

questions.prompt: Towns with more firefighters on duty tend to suffer more fire damage. The best reading of this is that...
options: a lurking variable, the size of the fire, drives both
the correlation is a pure coincidence
the town should hire fewer firefighters
questions.explanation: Bigger fires summon more firefighters and also cause more damage - the fire size is a common cause of both.

questions.prompt: The single feature that lets a randomized experiment support a causal claim is that...
options: it uses a very large sample
randomly assigning the treatment balances other factors across groups
it is cheaper than a survey
the researchers already know the answer
questions.explanation: Random assignment tends to spread confounders evenly, so a later difference points to the treatment itself.

questions.prompt: A confounding (lurking) variable is one that...
options: influences both the supposed cause and the effect
is the same as the outcome
questions.explanation: A confounder is a third factor tied to both variables, creating an association that is not itself causal.

questions.prompt: An online poll on a car-lovers forum finds most people plan to buy a new car soon. The main problem is...
options: the sample is too small to matter
selection bias - the respondents are not representative
questions.explanation: People on a car forum are unusually car-minded, so the sample is not representative of everyone.

questions.prompt: A disease is present in 1 percent of people. A test flags 99 percent of sick people and wrongly flags 5 percent of healthy people. Someone tests positive. Roughly how likely are they to be sick?
questions.explanation: Because healthy people vastly outnumber sick ones, most positives are false alarms - this is the base-rate effect.

questions.prompt: P(A given B) means...
options: the chance of A and B both happening
the chance of A once we know B happened
the chance of A or B
the chance of B given A
questions.explanation: A conditional probability restricts attention to the cases where B is true, then asks how often A holds among those.

questions.prompt: A treatment can look better in every subgroup yet worse overall. This reversal is called...
questions.explanation: Simpson's paradox happens when an ignored grouping variable is distributed very unevenly across the compared groups.

questions.prompt: A student scores far above their usual level on one test, then scores lower next time. The most likely explanation is...
options: regression to the mean - extreme scores tend to be followed by more ordinary ones
the first score was a lie
questions.explanation: An unusually high score owes part of itself to good luck, which does not repeat, so the next score drifts back toward average.

lessons.title: Correlation is not causation
lessons.grammar_note: Two variables can move together for four different reasons: A causes B, B causes A, a third thing causes both, or it is chance. A correlation alone cannot tell you which.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read a reported association and list the rival explanations before accepting a causal story. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, why do towns with more firefighters see more fire damage even though firefighters do not cause damage?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Two measurements are correlated when they tend to rise and fall together (positive) or in opposite directions (negative). Correlation is a description of a pattern, not an explanation of it. Whenever you see that X and Y move together, at least four stories could be true: X causes Y; Y causes X (reverse causation); some third variable Z causes both (confounding); or the match is a coincidence, especially with small samples or many variables tested. Good reasoning does not pick the flattering story by default - it keeps all four on the table until evidence rules some out. The strength of a correlation says nothing about which story is right; a very strong correlation can still be pure confounding.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Ice cream sales and drowning deaths rise together across the year. Ice cream does not drown anyone; hot weather is a common cause that raises both swimming and ice cream buying. Reverse causation: people who exercise report better mood, but calmer people may also be the ones with energy to exercise, so the arrow may point the other way, or both. Coincidence: over a decade, the number of films a certain actor appears in might track national cheese consumption almost perfectly; test enough unrelated pairs and some will line up by luck alone. In each case the numbers really do move together - the mistake is jumping straight to 'the first thing causes the second.'

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: For each pattern, name the most plausible non-causal explanation. 1) Children with bigger shoes read better. 2) Countries that eat more chocolate win more science prizes. 3) People who use sunscreen get more skin cancer. 4) Homes with more books raise higher-scoring students. 5) Sleeping with shoes on is linked to waking with a headache. Answers: 1) Age is a common cause - older children have bigger feet and read better. 2) Wealth drives both chocolate spending and research funding. 3) Sun exposure confounds it - sun-seekers use more sunscreen and get more sun. 4) Family income and education raise both book counts and scores. 5) Going to bed drunk causes both, a common cause.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating a strong or long-running correlation as proof of cause. Mistake: forgetting reverse causation, where the effect you named is actually the cause. Exit: (a) Name the four explanations for any correlation. (b) In the ice cream and drowning case, what is the common cause? Answers: X causes Y, Y causes X, a third variable causes both, or coincidence; hot weather.

lessons.title: Confounding and lurking variables
lessons.grammar_note: A confounder must be linked to the supposed cause AND be a cause of the outcome. If a variable fails either test, it is not confounding the relationship.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Identify a confounder, explain how it manufactures a false association, and describe how researchers try to remove its influence. Warm-up: what two conditions must a variable meet to count as a confounder?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A confounding variable, also called a lurking variable, is a third factor that is associated with the supposed cause and is itself a genuine cause of the outcome. When a confounder is present and ignored, the cause and effect appear linked even if the cause does nothing. Consider a claimed link between coffee drinking and heart disease. Smoking is associated with coffee drinking (many smokers drink coffee) and smoking causes heart disease. So coffee and heart disease can look linked purely through smoking. Researchers fight confounders three ways: control, by comparing only people with the same value of the confounder (compare smokers to smokers, non-smokers to non-smokers); adjustment, by using a model to statistically hold the confounder fixed; and best of all randomization, which spreads all confounders, even ones nobody thought of, roughly evenly across groups.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A study finds people who take a daily vitamin live longer. Health-consciousness is a likely confounder: careful people both take vitamins and exercise, eat well, and see doctors. When the vitamin group is compared only to equally health-conscious non-takers, the gap may vanish. A 2x2 table shows the trap. Among 200 people, suppose 60 of 100 vitamin-takers stay healthy (60 percent) versus 40 of 100 non-takers (40 percent). Looks like the vitamin works. But split by exercise: among exercisers, vitamin-takers 54 of 80 (68 percent) and non-takers 20 of 30 (67 percent) - nearly equal. Among non-exercisers, 6 of 20 (30 percent) versus 20 of 70 (29 percent) - also nearly equal. The whole gap came from vitamin-takers exercising more. Exercise was the lurking cause.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) A city notes neighborhoods with more parks have lower obesity; name a confounder. 2) What two conditions define a confounder? 3) Which method removes confounders you never thought to measure? 4) A study says wine drinkers have fewer heart attacks; give one confounder. 5) True or false: adjusting for a confounder requires you to have measured it. Answers: 1) Income - wealthier areas have both more parks and residents with more time and money for health. 2) It must be associated with the supposed cause and be a real cause of the outcome. 3) Randomization. 4) Income, moderate lifestyle, or that light drinkers are healthier to begin with. 5) True - you can only adjust for variables you actually recorded.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: calling any correlated variable a confounder, even one that sits between cause and effect on the causal path (that is a mediator, not a confounder). Mistake: assuming statistical adjustment fixes everything, when it only handles confounders you measured. Exit: (a) Why is randomization stronger than adjustment? (b) In the vitamin table, what was the true driver? Answers: randomization balances even unknown and unmeasured confounders; exercise.

lessons.title: Experiments versus observational studies
lessons.grammar_note: In an experiment the researcher assigns who gets the treatment; in an observational study people or nature decide. That single difference is what licenses causal language.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Tell an experiment from an observational study and explain why random assignment, a control group, and blinding let an experiment support cause-and-effect claims. Warm-up: who decides who gets the treatment in an experiment versus an observational study?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: In an observational study you watch and record; the participants, or nature, decide who is exposed to the supposed cause. Because exposure is self-selected, confounders are almost always present, so observational studies establish association, not causation. In a designed experiment the researcher assigns the treatment, ideally at random. Random assignment is the engine: it tends to balance every other factor across the treatment and control groups, so a later difference in outcomes can be pinned on the treatment. Three ingredients strengthen an experiment. A control group receives no treatment or a placebo, giving a baseline to compare against. Randomization decides who lands in each group, balancing confounders. Blinding hides who got what - from participants (single-blind) and ideally from the people measuring outcomes (double-blind) - to keep expectations from bending the results.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Observational: researchers follow 1,000 adults and find those who take long walks have lower blood pressure. Tempting, but people who can take long walks may be healthier already - confounded. Experimental version: recruit 1,000 similar adults, randomly assign 500 to a daily walking program and 500 to usual routine, measure blood pressure after six months. Now the walking group and control group started balanced, so a lower average in the walkers points to the walking. The placebo effect shows why control and blinding matter: in drug trials, people given a sugar pill often improve simply because they expect to. Only by comparing the real drug against a placebo, with neither patients nor assessors knowing which is which, can you separate the drug's effect from expectation.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) A survey links vegetable eating to longevity - experiment or observational? 2) What does a control group provide? 3) Why double-blind rather than single-blind? 4) You randomly assign students to two study apps and compare test scores - experiment or observational? 5) Name the feature of experiments that balances unknown confounders. Answers: 1) Observational - no one assigned diets. 2) A baseline showing what happens without the treatment. 3) It also blinds the people measuring outcomes, preventing biased assessment. 4) Experiment - you assigned the treatment. 5) Random assignment.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reporting an observational finding with causal words like 'causes' or 'reduces.' Mistake: thinking a huge observational sample can substitute for randomization - size does not remove confounding. Exit: (a) What makes an experiment able to support a causal claim? (b) What is the purpose of a placebo? Answers: random assignment of the treatment; to provide a comparison that holds expectation and attention constant so the treatment's own effect stands out.

questions.prompt: A newspaper reports that students who drink milk score higher on math tests. Before believing milk helps, you should first suspect...
options: a confounder such as family income
the math test was too easy
questions.explanation: Wealthier families may buy more milk and provide more academic support - see 'Confounding and lurking variables.'

questions.prompt: The defining difference between an experiment and an observational study is that in an experiment...
questions.explanation: Assignment of the treatment, ideally at random, is what separates the two designs.

questions.prompt: Random assignment mainly protects against...
questions.explanation: Randomizing tends to balance all other factors across groups, even ones nobody measured.

questions.prompt: Sunscreen use is positively correlated with skin cancer. The lurking variable is most likely...
questions.explanation: People in the sun more use more sunscreen and also get more cancer-causing exposure - a common cause.

questions.prompt: A double-blind design means...
options: neither the participants nor the assessors know who got the treatment
questions.explanation: Hiding assignment from both sides blocks expectations from shaping and measuring the outcome.

questions.prompt: Which of these can an observational study, by itself, legitimately claim?
options: that X and Y are associated
that removing X will remove Y
questions.explanation: Without assignment, observational data show association, not causation.

lessons.title: Sampling and bias
lessons.grammar_note: A big sample is not the same as a representative sample. Adding more people from the wrong group makes the bias more precise, not more true.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Judge whether a sample can speak for its population and name the common ways samples go wrong. Warm-up: a call-in radio poll gets 50,000 responses - does the large number make it trustworthy?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A statistic is only as good as the sample it came from. The target population is everyone the claim is about; the sample is who was actually measured. A sample is representative when it looks like the population in the ways that matter. The gold standard is a random sample, where every member has a known chance of selection, because randomness prevents systematic tilt. Bias is any systematic gap between sample and population. Selection bias comes from how people enter the sample: convenience samples, self-selected online polls, and volunteer studies all over-represent whoever is easiest or keenest to reach. Non-response bias arises when the people who ignore a survey differ from those who answer. Survivorship bias looks only at the cases that made it through, ignoring those that dropped out. Response bias comes from leading questions or from people answering how they think they should.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A famous 1936 magazine poll mailed millions of ballots to its subscribers and to car and telephone owners, predicting a landslide for one presidential candidate; the other candidate won easily. In 1936 owning a car or phone signaled wealth, so the sample leaned one way - a selection bias no sample size could fix. Survivorship: during wartime, engineers examined returning planes and wanted to armor the spots most often hit. The reasoning reversed once someone noted the planes that were hit in other spots never returned to be examined; the untouched areas on survivors were exactly where armor was needed. Response bias: 'Don't you agree our overworked nurses deserve a raise?' will draw more yeses than a neutral wording, because the question pushes.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) A website asks visitors to rate its own service; why is the sample biased? 2) What kind of bias is a war-plane armor study prone to? 3) Does raising a biased sample from 500 to 5,000 people fix the bias? 4) A survey mailed out gets only a 12 percent reply; what bias threatens it? 5) Rewrite 'Wouldn't you love a cleaner city?' to be neutral. Answers: 1) Selection or self-selection bias - visitors, and especially the strongly opinionated, are not typical. 2) Survivorship bias. 3) No - more data just sharpens the same wrong estimate. 4) Non-response bias, since the 88 percent who ignored it may differ. 5) 'How satisfied are you with the cleanliness of the city?'

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: trusting a poll because it has many responses, ignoring how those responders were chosen. Mistake: studying only survivors - customers who stayed, patients who returned - and missing those who left. Exit: (a) What makes a sample representative? (b) Name the bias in a voluntary online poll. Answers: it resembles the population in the traits that matter, best ensured by random selection; selection or self-selection bias.

lessons.title: Rates, base rates, and the base-rate fallacy
lessons.grammar_note: A percentage always has a hidden denominator. '90 percent of positives are correct' and '90 percent of the sick test positive' are different claims - always ask, percent of what?

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read a rate correctly, keep track of the denominator, and use base rates to judge how much a positive result really means. Warm-up: if a test catches 99 percent of a rare disease, why might a positive result still usually be a false alarm?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A rate is a count divided by a total, and its meaning lives in the total. The base rate of a condition is how common it is in the whole population before any test. The base-rate fallacy is ignoring that background frequency and judging a positive result only by the test's accuracy. When a condition is rare, even a small false-positive rate applied to the huge healthy majority can produce more false positives than true ones. The cleanest way to see this is to imagine a concrete crowd - say 10,000 people - and count. Turning percentages into counts of real people, sometimes drawn as a tree, makes the answer obvious where raw percentages mislead. Two numbers describe a test: sensitivity, the share of truly positive cases it catches, and specificity, the share of truly negative cases it correctly clears. One minus specificity is the false-positive rate.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A disease affects 1 percent of people. A test has 99 percent sensitivity and 95 percent specificity (a 5 percent false-positive rate). Take 10,000 people. About 100 have the disease; the test flags 99 of them (true positives). The other 9,900 are healthy; 5 percent, or 495, are wrongly flagged (false positives). Total positives: 99 plus 495 equals 594. So the chance a positive person is actually sick is 99 divided by 594, about 17 percent - despite a test that sounds 99 percent accurate. Now raise the base rate: if 30 percent of the tested group is sick, then 3,000 sick give 2,970 true positives and 7,000 healthy give 350 false positives, so a positive means 2,970 of 3,320, about 89 percent. Same test, very different meaning, because the base rate changed.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Use a crowd of 10,000. A condition affects 2 percent; the test has 90 percent sensitivity and 90 percent specificity. 1) How many people have the condition? 2) How many true positives? 3) How many healthy people, and how many false positives? 4) Total positives? 5) Chance a positive person truly has it? Answers: 1) 2 percent of 10,000 = 200. 2) 90 percent of 200 = 180. 3) 9,800 healthy; 10 percent wrongly flagged = 980 false positives. 4) 180 + 980 = 1,160. 5) 180 / 1,160 = about 15.5 percent - again most positives are false because the condition is rare.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading '99 percent accurate' as 'a positive is 99 percent likely to be real' - that confuses sensitivity with the chance of disease given a positive. Mistake: ignoring the base rate entirely. Exit: (a) Why can a positive on an accurate test still probably be wrong? (b) What does specificity measure? Answers: when the condition is rare, false positives from the large healthy group can outnumber true positives; the share of truly negative cases the test correctly clears.

lessons.title: Conditional probability and updating beliefs
lessons.grammar_note: P(A given B) and P(B given A) are not the same. Confusing them is the prosecutor's fallacy: the chance of the evidence if innocent is not the chance of innocence given the evidence.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: State a conditional probability precisely, avoid swapping the two directions, and update a belief when new evidence arrives. Warm-up: 'the chance of a positive test if you are sick' and 'the chance you are sick if the test is positive' - are these the same number?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A conditional probability P(A given B) is the chance of A once we know B has happened; it narrows attention to the world where B is true and asks how often A holds there. Two directions, P(A given B) and P(B given A), are usually different, and treating them as equal is a classic error. Updating a belief means starting from a prior, the base rate you held before the evidence, and revising it in light of how strongly the evidence points one way. The recipe in plain terms: begin with how common the hypothesis is, weigh how much more likely the evidence is when the hypothesis is true than when it is false, and land on a revised belief. Strong evidence moves you a lot; but a very low prior, a rare hypothesis, keeps the revised belief modest, which is exactly the base-rate lesson seen again through the lens of updating.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Direction matters. Almost every person who has a certain rare disease shows a specific symptom, so P(symptom given disease) is near 1. That does not mean P(disease given symptom) is near 1 - plenty of healthy people have the symptom too, and the disease is rare. Updating with counts: return to the 1 percent disease with a 99 percent sensitive, 95 percent specific test. Prior belief of disease: 1 percent. After a positive test, we computed the revised belief as 99 of 594, about 17 percent. The positive test raised the belief seventeen-fold, from 1 percent to 17 percent, yet it stays well under half because the starting point was so low. A second independent positive would raise it much further, since we would now start updating from 17 percent, not 1 percent.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which is usually larger for a rare disease: P(symptom given disease) or P(disease given symptom)? 2) In updating, what does the prior represent? 3) If evidence is equally likely whether or not the hypothesis is true, how much should your belief change? 4) A positive test moved a belief from 1 percent to 17 percent; a second positive starts updating from which number? 5) Name the fallacy of swapping P(evidence given innocent) for P(innocent given evidence). Answers: 1) P(symptom given disease). 2) The base rate, your belief before seeing the evidence. 3) Not at all - uninformative evidence leaves the belief where it was. 4) 17 percent. 5) The prosecutor's fallacy.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: flipping the conditional, reading P(evidence given hypothesis) as P(hypothesis given evidence). Mistake: forgetting the prior, so a strong-sounding test overwhelms a rare base rate. Exit: (a) What are the two directions of a conditional, and why do they differ? (b) Why does a positive test for a rare disease often leave the odds below 50 percent? Answers: P(A given B) versus P(B given A) differ because the two conditioning groups have different sizes; the low prior keeps the updated belief small even after strong evidence.

questions.prompt: A call-in poll receives 80,000 responses. Its biggest weakness is...
options: the respondents chose themselves and are not representative
questions.explanation: Self-selection makes the sample unrepresentative no matter how large - see 'Sampling and bias.'

questions.prompt: A disease affects 1 percent of people; a test is 99 percent sensitive and 95 percent specific. Out of 10,000, roughly how many positives are false alarms?
questions.explanation: 5 percent of the 9,900 healthy people, about 495, are wrongly flagged.

questions.prompt: The base-rate fallacy is the mistake of...
options: judging a positive result while ignoring how rare the condition is
questions.explanation: Ignoring the background frequency makes an accurate test look far more conclusive than it is.

questions.prompt: P(A given B) equals P(B given A)...
options: only in special cases, not in general
questions.explanation: The two directions condition on different-sized groups and are generally unequal.

questions.prompt: Studying only planes that returned from combat, or customers who stayed, risks...
questions.explanation: Looking only at survivors omits the cases that dropped out, distorting the picture.

questions.prompt: After a positive test raises the chance of disease from 1 percent to 17 percent, a second independent positive test should...
options: start updating from 17 percent and raise it further
questions.explanation: The revised 17 percent becomes the new prior for the next piece of evidence.

lessons.title: Simpson's paradox and regression to the mean
lessons.grammar_note: An aggregate can lie about its parts. Before trusting a combined rate, ask whether the groups being combined differ in some important way.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Recognize Simpson's paradox, explain the hidden grouping that causes it, and spot regression to the mean behind stories of decline or improvement. Warm-up: can a treatment win in every subgroup yet lose overall?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Simpson's paradox is a reversal: an association that holds in every subgroup flips when the subgroups are pooled. It happens when a lurking grouping variable is spread very unevenly across the compared groups, so the pooled numbers are dominated by whichever subgroup each group mostly falls into. The cure is to keep the relevant grouping visible rather than collapsing it. Regression to the mean is a different trap. Any measurement mixes a stable part with luck. An extreme result, high or low, usually got help from luck in that direction, and luck does not repeat, so the next measurement drifts back toward the average. This produces illusions of cause: the worst performers 'improve' after an intervention and the best 'decline,' even if the intervention did nothing, simply because extremes are followed by more ordinary values.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Two treatments for kidney stones. Treatment A cures 93 percent of small stones (81 of 87) and 73 percent of large stones (192 of 263). Treatment B cures 87 percent of small stones (234 of 270) and 69 percent of large stones (55 of 80). A beats B in both sizes. Yet overall A cures 273 of 350 (78 percent) while B cures 289 of 350 (83 percent), so B looks better pooled. The reason: doctors gave A to the hard large-stone cases and B mostly to easy small-stone cases, so B's overall rate rode on easy patients. Regression to the mean: a coach benches players after a great game and they play worse next time, 'proving' benching hurts; in truth a career-best game is partly luck, so an ordinary game naturally follows. A speed-camera placed where crashes spiked will see crashes fall afterward even if it does nothing, because the spike itself was partly random.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What condition on the grouping variable produces Simpson's paradox? 2) In the kidney-stone case, why did B win overall despite losing both subgroups? 3) A tutoring program targets the lowest scorers, who improve next term; what harmless explanation must be ruled out? 4) True or false: regression to the mean needs a cause to explain the change. 5) How do you avoid Simpson's paradox when reporting a rate? Answers: 1) It is distributed very unevenly across the compared groups. 2) B mostly treated easy small-stone cases, inflating its pooled rate. 3) Regression to the mean - extreme low scores tend to rise on their own. 4) False - it happens by chance alone, from luck not repeating. 5) Keep the relevant subgroups separate instead of pooling them blindly.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: trusting an overall rate without checking how subgroups are distributed. Mistake: crediting an intervention for improvement among extreme cases that would have regressed anyway. Exit: (a) What causes Simpson's paradox? (b) Why do the worst performers tend to improve even with no real treatment? Answers: an unevenly distributed lurking grouping variable that reverses the pooled result; their extreme scores were partly luck, and the next measurement drifts back toward the mean.

lessons.title: P-hacking and fallacies of evidence
lessons.grammar_note: A result that is 'statistically significant' means the data would be surprising if nothing were going on. It does not mean the effect is large, important, or real once you account for how many things were tested.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain why testing many hypotheses inflates false discoveries, recognize p-hacking and publication bias, and separate significance from importance. Warm-up: if you test 20 useless treatments at the usual threshold, how many might look significant by chance?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A p-value is the chance of seeing data at least this extreme if there were truly no effect. A common threshold calls a result significant when that chance is below 5 percent. But 5 percent is not zero: test twenty unrelated hypotheses and, on average, one will clear the bar by luck alone. This is the multiple-comparisons problem. P-hacking is squeezing a dataset until something crosses the threshold - trying many outcomes, splitting into subgroups, dropping inconvenient data points, or stopping collection the moment the result looks good - then reporting only the winner. Publication bias compounds it: studies that find an effect get published while null results sit in a drawer, so the visible literature overstates how often effects are real. Two more habits mislead: confusing statistical significance with practical importance (a tiny, useless effect can be significant in a huge sample), and reading a non-significant result as proof of no effect, when it may just mean too little data.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Jelly-bean scenario: a team tests whether jelly beans cause acne and finds nothing. They then test 20 individual colors separately. One color, by luck, comes back significant at the 5 percent level, and a headline announces that color causes acne. With 20 tests, about one false positive is expected - the finding is noise dressed as discovery. P-hacking by stopping: researchers peek at the data every few subjects and stop the instant the p-value dips below 5 percent; this almost guarantees crossing the line eventually even with no real effect. Significance versus size: with a million users, an app change that lifts clicks from 10.00 percent to 10.02 percent can be highly significant yet far too small to matter. The honest defenses are pre-registration (declaring the single planned test in advance), correcting for the number of comparisons, and replication in fresh data.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Testing 40 useless hypotheses at the 5 percent level, how many false positives are expected by chance? 2) Name two p-hacking moves. 3) Does a very small p-value guarantee a large effect? 4) Why does publication bias make the literature look too positive? 5) What practice best guards against p-hacking? Answers: 1) About 2 (5 percent of 40). 2) Testing many outcomes and keeping the best; stopping data collection when significant; subgroup fishing; dropping outliers to taste. 3) No - significance is about surprise, not size; huge samples make tiny effects significant. 4) Null results go unpublished, so only the effect-finding studies are visible. 5) Pre-registering the hypothesis and analysis before seeing the data, plus replication.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading a single significant result without asking how many tests were run to get it. Mistake: equating 'significant' with 'big' or 'important.' Exit: (a) Why does testing many hypotheses produce false positives? (b) What does a non-significant result actually tell you? Answers: at a 5 percent threshold, about 1 in 20 useless tests clears the bar by luck; that this study did not find enough evidence for an effect, not that the effect is zero.

lessons.title: Reading graphs and claims critically
lessons.grammar_note: The same numbers can tell opposite stories depending on the axis, the baseline, and whether a figure is a raw count, a rate, or a change. Always find the denominator and the scale before reacting.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Interrogate a chart or a headline number: check the axis, the baseline, the denominator, and what is being compared. Warm-up: a bar looks twice as tall as its neighbor - what should you check before believing it means twice as much?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Graphs and stated figures are arguments, and they can be built to persuade rather than inform. A truncated axis that does not start at zero can turn a tiny difference into a dramatic cliff. A dual axis can force two unrelated lines to appear to track each other. Absolute numbers and relative numbers tell different stories: 'risk doubled' sounds alarming until you learn it went from 1 in a million to 2 in a million. Cherry-picked time ranges hide a trend by starting or ending at a convenient point. Missing denominators turn meaningless counts into false alarms - a rise in total cases may just reflect a growing population or more testing. Good practice is a short checklist: What is measured, exactly? Per what - the denominator? Compared to what baseline? Over what time window, and why that window? And does the visual scale match the real magnitude?

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Truncated axis: a chart of a company's sales with the vertical axis running from 98 to 102 makes a 1 percent rise look like a doubling; redrawn from zero, the bars are nearly equal. Relative versus absolute: 'this food raises your risk of a rare cancer by 50 percent' may mean the lifetime risk rose from 2 in 10,000 to 3 in 10,000 - a real but tiny absolute change. Missing denominator: 'more left-handed people die in accidents involving right-handed tools' ignores that left-handers are a minority; the rate per left-hander is what matters. Cherry-picked window: a temperature or price chart can show 'decline' by starting at an unusually high year; extend the window and the trend reverses. In each case the underlying numbers are honest; the framing does the misleading.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) A bar chart's y-axis starts at 90 instead of 0; what is the risk? 2) A drug 'cuts risk by 50 percent' from 2 in 100,000 to 1 in 100,000 - is the absolute change large? 3) Why demand a denominator when told 'accidents rose by 300 last year'? 4) A stock chart starts at its highest-ever month; what bias is that? 5) List two questions from the critical-reading checklist. Answers: 1) Small differences look huge because the axis is truncated. 2) No - the absolute drop is 1 in 100,000, tiny in everyday terms. 3) The count may reflect a bigger population or more reporting; the rate per person is what matters. 4) Cherry-picking the time window. 5) Per what (denominator)? Compared to what baseline? Also: over what time range, and does the scale match the magnitude?

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reacting to a relative change without asking the absolute baseline. Mistake: trusting the visual height of a bar or steepness of a line without reading the axis. Exit: (a) Why can a truncated axis mislead? (b) What single question defuses most scary raw counts? Answers: it exaggerates small differences by not starting at zero; 'per what?' - find the denominator, since a rate often tells a calmer story than the count.

questions.prompt: Treatment A beats Treatment B for both small and large stones, yet B has the higher overall cure rate. This is...
questions.explanation: An unevenly distributed grouping variable, stone size, reverses the pooled result - see 'Simpson's paradox and regression to the mean.'

questions.prompt: A program targets the lowest-scoring students, who improve next term. A harmless explanation to rule out first is...
questions.explanation: Extreme low scores tend to rise on their own as luck fails to repeat.

questions.prompt: Testing 20 useless hypotheses at the 5 percent significance level, the expected number of false positives is about...
questions.explanation: 5 percent of 20 is 1, so roughly one will look significant by chance.

questions.prompt: A very small p-value in a study of a million users tells you the effect is...
options: surprising if nothing were going on, but possibly tiny
certainly real and worth acting on
questions.explanation: Significance is about surprise, not size; huge samples make tiny effects significant.

questions.prompt: A bar chart whose vertical axis starts at 90 rather than 0 tends to...
questions.explanation: Truncating the axis makes minor gaps look dramatic.

questions.prompt: 'This food raises your cancer risk by 50 percent.' The most important follow-up question is...
options: what does the food taste like
50 percent of what baseline risk, in absolute terms
questions.explanation: A relative rise is meaningless without the absolute baseline it applies to.

lessons.title: Capstone: evaluate a real-world claim
lessons.grammar_note: A good evaluation does not just declare a claim true or false; it names the study design, the rival explanations, and what evidence would change the verdict.

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Take one causal claim from a headline, advertisement, or social feed - for example, 'People who drink coffee live longer' or 'Students who use this app score higher.' Write a short structured evaluation that walks through every tool in this course, ending with a calibrated verdict rather than a flat yes or no. Do not merely agree or disagree; show the reasoning that leads there.

sections.heading: The structure to follow
sections.text: 1) State the claim precisely and identify the supposed cause and effect. 2) Design: is the evidence an experiment or observational? Who assigned the treatment? 3) Confounders: list at least two lurking variables that could explain the link, and say whether the study controlled for them. 4) Sample: who was measured, how were they selected, and what bias threatens the sample? 5) Numbers: are figures given as rates with clear denominators; is any base rate being ignored; is a relative change hiding a tiny absolute one? 6) Fallacies: could Simpson's paradox, regression to the mean, or p-hacking be at work? 7) Verdict: state how much the evidence should move your belief, and name the one piece of evidence that would most change your mind.

sections.heading: A worked model of a different claim
sections.text: Claim: 'Employees who attend the optional wellness program take fewer sick days, so the program improves health.' Design: observational - employees chose to attend, so no random assignment. Confounders: health-consciousness (already-healthy people opt in) and job type (flexible, lower-stress roles allow both attendance and fewer absences); the report did not control for either. Sample: only current employees who volunteered, so self-selection and survivorship bias loom - those who quit or were often sick may be absent from the data. Numbers: 'fewer sick days' lacks a baseline; is it 4 versus 5 days, and per what period? Fallacies: regression to the mean is plausible if the program recruited people right after a bad-health spell. Verdict: the association is real but weak evidence for cause; my belief that the program itself improves health should rise only slightly. What would change my mind: a randomized trial assigning similar employees to the program or a control, showing fewer sick days in the treated group. Use this as a template of tone and thoroughness - do not copy it; run your own chosen claim through the same seven steps.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Quick self-checks before you write. 1) If the study is observational, what word should you avoid in your verdict? 2) Name two confounders for 'coffee drinkers live longer.' 3) If a claim reports 'risk doubled,' what number must you find? 4) Which fallacy should you suspect when the studied group was chosen for being extreme? 5) What single design would most strengthen a shaky causal claim? Answers: 1) 'Causes' - say 'is associated with' instead. 2) Smoking status and overall wealth or lifestyle, both tied to coffee habits and to health. 3) The absolute baseline risk the doubling applies to. 4) Regression to the mean. 5) A randomized controlled experiment.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: Check yes to each: you stated the claim and its cause-effect direction; you classified the design as experimental or observational and said who assigned the treatment; you named at least two plausible confounders; you described who was sampled and one sampling bias; you checked the numbers for denominators, base rates, and relative-versus-absolute framing; you considered at least one named fallacy; and you ended with a calibrated verdict plus the one piece of evidence that would change it. If all seven are true, you have evaluated the claim like a careful reasoner rather than a headline reader.

questions.prompt: The four possible explanations for any correlation between X and Y are X causes Y, Y causes X, coincidence, and...
questions.explanation: Confounding by a common cause is the fourth explanation you must always keep on the table.

questions.prompt: The two conditions a variable must meet to be a confounder are being associated with the supposed cause and...
options: being a genuine cause of the outcome
questions.explanation: A confounder must both track the cause and actually affect the outcome.

questions.prompt: What single feature lets an experiment support a causal claim that an observational study cannot?
questions.explanation: Random assignment balances confounders across groups so a difference can be pinned on the treatment.

questions.prompt: A 1936 magazine poll failed despite millions of responses because...
options: of selection bias toward wealthier respondents
questions.explanation: Sampling car and phone owners tilted the sample; size cannot fix a biased frame.

questions.prompt: A disease affects 1 percent; a test is 99 percent sensitive and 95 percent specific. Given a positive result, the chance of disease is closest to...
questions.explanation: In 10,000 people, 99 true positives against 495 false positives give 99/594, about 17 percent.

questions.prompt: Reading P(positive given sick) as if it were P(sick given positive) is...
options: confusing the two directions of a conditional
questions.explanation: The two conditionals point in opposite directions and are generally unequal.

questions.prompt: A treatment that wins in every subgroup but loses overall illustrates...
questions.explanation: An unevenly distributed grouping variable reverses the pooled result.

questions.prompt: The worst-performing branches improve after a new manager visits only them. Before crediting the manager, suspect...
questions.explanation: Extreme low results tend to drift back toward average on their own.

questions.prompt: Running 20 subgroup tests and reporting only the one that reached significance is an example of...
questions.explanation: About 1 in 20 useless tests clears a 5 percent threshold by chance, so cherry-picking the winner manufactures a false finding.

questions.prompt: 'This supplement cuts your risk by 40 percent.' The essential missing information is...
questions.explanation: A relative change is uninterpretable without the absolute risk it modifies.

questions.prompt: A bar chart whose y-axis begins at 95 instead of 0 is designed to...
questions.explanation: A truncated axis inflates minor gaps into dramatic-looking ones.

questions.prompt: When evaluating an observational claim, the correct verdict language is...
questions.explanation: Without random assignment, the honest claim is association, not causation.
